rationale: Early cleavage is influenced by yolk and cortex mechanics, but later cleavage planes are set by spindles, cytoskeletal polarity and inherited determinants. Simple surface-tension laws do not fix the whole configuration at every stage, as invariant lineages and regulated cleavage show.

Polar-furrow geometry does shift with the relative sizes of the four blastomeres, and the same geometric arrangements turn up in unrelated embryos. Those size ratios are themselves often clade-typical, so the patterns are not distributed without relation to classification.
Developmental form is produced by physical forces, including molecular and cytoskeletal ones, at every stage. There is no evidence that an agency outside physics takes over from those forces.

Among equal-volume cuts of a rectangular cell, the least-area partition is perpendicular to the longest axis. Successive cuts need not be at right angles: a very long cell keeps dividing across the same axis, so the new walls stay parallel.

Plant cell plates often lie close to a least-area surface, and the rectangular right-angle rule is the special case of that geometry. It is a tendency, not the fundamental rule of cell division: spindles, preprophase bands and asymmetric divisions frequently override it, especially in animal blastomeres.

For a cube, a quarter-cylindrical cut along an edge has less area than a face-parallel plane once the smaller volume drops below about three-tenths, and a spherical octant becomes smaller still below about 0.15. Curved walls in strongly unequal plant divisions match that geometry, though cells do not always adopt the global minimum.

The shortest equal-area wall of a circular quadrant, meeting the radius and the rim at right angles, is a circular arc that leaves the side near three-tenths of the radius and meets the rim near 55°22′. Flattened algal cells and pressure-flattened eggs often divide this way, but not invariably.

In a circular sector the equal-area anticlinal wall is shorter than the equal-area periclinal wall only when the angle is wider than about 62.5°, up to a right angle. Cells that minimise wall area tend to follow that switch, with many developmental exceptions.

Under uniform enlargement of a disc, areas of material regions scale by the same factor, so equal triangular and quadrilateral halves do not gain area at different rates. Asynchronous division is common for other reasons, but the stated radius factors of about 1.345 and 1.517 do not follow from similar growth.

Repeated area-minimising divisions of a disc can leave a more regular peripheral layer of quadrilateral cells. A biological epidermis is a differentiated tissue, not the automatic product of that packing, though some algal discs look superficially similar.

With every cell on the boundary and only triple junctions, adjacency graphs of an eight-cell disc are a small finite set, and an enumeration into thirteen types is combinatorially plausible. Real embryos sometimes include internal cells or four-way junctions, which fall outside that classification.

In small soap-bubble clusters, lower-energy arrangements spread contacts fairly evenly, and highly centralised contact patterns are unstable. Embryonic cell groups are only partly selected that way, because division order and adhesion bias which topologies appear.

At the frog eight-cell stage the animal-pole furrows take more than one arrangement, so a single partition pattern is not a fixed species character there. Many other animals, especially spiral-cleaving and mosaic embryos, do have a highly constant eight-cell geometry.

A surface divided into few faces really does admit only a few topologies, so some cell arrangements recur widely. Cleavage patterns and organ layouts still track classification, so recurrence is not independent of phylogeny.

A rugose-coral fossula is tied to the cardinal septum and the bilateral plan of septal insertion, not merely to one accidental triple junction of septa. Treating it as no evidence of bilaterality understates that organisation.

Stomata commonly lie in files where epidermal cells are oblong, as in many monocot leaves, and are scattered where the epidermis is polygonal. Patterning is mainly by oriented files and inhibitory signalling; the minimal-partition geometry of the mother cell is only a contributing constraint.

Tetrad geometry imprints proximal faces and aperture patterns when the wall stiffens before the grains separate, as in trilete spores and many pollen grains. Grains that remain plastic round up, though later exine sculpting can modify either outcome.

Tissue-level growth can be robust to changes in cell size and division pattern, so the cell net is often partly a consequence of overall form. Oriented divisions, anisotropic expansion and proliferation rates also cause shape, so the network is not merely a result.

Apical cells of mosses, liverworts and many algae tend to divide across their long axis, so the plane does track the shape reached before mitosis, which depends on how fast the cell grows relative to how often it divides. The hemisphere rules are only approximate, and the preprophase band can set a plane the shape alone would not.

Cryptogam apical cells are often triangular or tetrahedral and are the source of the shoot, and some branch initials arise from particular segments. Bud position is not generally explained by periclinal walls stiffening quadrangular cells while oblique walls let triangular cells bulge out.

Bone, molluscan shell and many spicules mineralise in extracellular matrix rather than in bulk cytoplasm. Plenty of skeletons form inside living cells or membrane-bound compartments, and even extracellular mineral is shaped by cells and organic matrix, so form is not independent of the living tissue.

Echinoid embryos reared without dissolved calcium fail to deposit larval skeletal rods, and the pluteus arms that those rods distend do not form, while early development otherwise proceeds. The larva is impaired rather than fully normal, and the extension to every skeleton-bearing organism is much less secure.

Biological homochirality need not be a special power of life; abiotic routes to an enantiomeric excess are physically possible. Sunlight circularly polarised by reflection from the sea is a very weak asymmetry and is not a credible source of the biological excess, though other non-living asymmetries remain possible.

Pearls and otoliths are concentrically layered and often radially textured, as are carbonate spherulites grown in protein gels. Their ultrastructure and the control of deposition differ from passive precipitation in albumin, so the shared look does not show the same mode of formation.

Diffusion-limited precipitation can make concentric bands without any external clock, so rhythm alone is not proof of seasons or days. In otoliths, fish scales and bone, validated daily and annual increments do record external and physiological cycles, so the blanket refusal to treat them as such is not warranted.

Skeletal calcium is not thrown down because albumin is catabolised and stops holding the salts in solution. Mineralisation is controlled by matrix, phosphate chemistry and inhibitors, and the older carbonic-acid story is not replaced by that protein-breakdown account.

At cell-sized scales, surface and molecular forces dominate skeletal shape, whereas gravity and muscle loads dominate the architecture of large bones. The contrast of scale is real, even though small spicules are also genetically templated and bone is not shaped by mechanics alone.

A straight rod forced to stay on a surface does follow a geodesic: a great-circle arc on a sphere, not a space spiral, and an S-shaped curve is not a geodesic of a convex cell. Some C-shaped spicules could fit an arc, but sigmas and similar spicules are built by sclerocytes rather than by that constraint alone.

Holothurian calcite ossicles and siliceous sponge spicules share some broad shapes, such as rods, anchors and wheels, so lattice chemistry does not uniquely dictate those outlines. The resemblance is not often identity, and crystal habit plus cellular secretion still shape both.

Equal triple junctions sit at 120°, and the tetrahedral angle is about 109°, and calcareous-sponge triradiates and tetractines often lie near those values. Secretion in the space among a few sclerocytes can produce that geometry, but the rays are actively positioned rather than simply frozen cell corners, and unequal or curved rays are common.

Hexactinellid megascleres are typically orthogonal six-rayed spicules, so the cubic symmetry of the form is real. Soft vesicles pack in a close-packed, not cubic, arrangement unless forced, and silica deposition by the sponge syncytium is not explained by cubic vesicle packing.

A small sediment sample can contain many radiolarian species at once. Species nevertheless have oceanographic ranges, assemblages are locally dominated by a few forms, and genera turn over through time rather than standing unchanged since the Cambrian.

A spherical mesh cannot be a purely regular hexagonal net; twelve pentagons are required, and radiolarian lattices show that mixture. Silica is patterned by a cytoplasmic template, not simply by draining into grooves between equal surface bubbles, though a vesicular cortex may influence the mesh.

Lattice-like skeletons occur in silica, in strontium sulphate and in organic capsules, so material does not uniquely fix a reticulate habit. Acantharian skeletons are chiefly radial spicules of a crystal with its own symmetry, and the organic heliozoan capsule is not an equally regular hexagonal shell moulded the same way.

Four bubbles in tetrahedral contact do meet in six films at 120°, with edges near 109°, and the Callimitra skeleton has a similar faceted look. Nassellarian silica is laid down on a cytoplasmic mould, which does not establish that the skeleton had to form on the interfaces of four cells.

Foreign grains do stick in the surface coat of testate amoebae and agglutinated foraminifera, so surface energy plays a part. Species select grain size and often mineral type and place particles with pseudopodia, which passive trapping by specific surface energies does not account for.

A periodic crystal cannot have the five-fold symmetry of a regular dodecahedron or icosahedron, so those forms are not crystal space-fillings. Radiolarian skeletons approximate several regular polyhedra, though the perfect solids in older drawings are idealised, and the conclusion still holds for genuine five-fold cages.

The twenty spines of acantharians follow Müller's arrangement of five zones of four spines, with four-fold spacing around the equator rather than six equatorial rays and two polar spines. A hexagonal reading does not fit the observed skeleton, and the four-spine rule applies throughout the group.

The fixed latitudes of radiolarian spines are organised from the central cell and its axopods, not by the mechanics of a peripheral froth. Ordering forces of the liquid-crystal type are a possible physical analogue, but they remain an unspecified suggestion rather than a demonstrated cause.

Geodesics on a cylinder are circles, longitudinal generators and helices, and annular, longitudinal and spiral wall thickenings of vessels realise those three. Insect tracheae likewise carry a helical thread, which is the geodesic coil on a tube.

A geodesic on a cone does spiral tighter toward the apex, because it is a straight line on the unrolled sector. The suture of a regular turreted shell is a constant-angle logarithmic spiral on that cone, and a logarithmic spiral is not a geodesic except in degenerate cases.

Opposite helical geodesics on a cylinder cross in a regular lattice, and paired spiral thickenings do that on some cell walls and tubes. Most reticulate organic patterns, including netted vessel thickenings, are not produced by two interfering geodesic families.

On a cylindrical organ, circular, longitudinal and helical fibres are geodesics, and gut, vessel and worm muscle is largely laid down that way. Fibres are embedded and developmentally oriented rather than free to shorten onto a geodesic, and the heart's transmural fibre angle is more complex than that automatic picture.

The heart and stomach do arise by bending and dilating a tube, and oblique gastric fibres exist. A geodesic on the original tube does not remain a geodesic after an arbitrary twist, and cardiac ejection depends on helical fibre architecture and activation, not on fibres taking the shortest path.

Rotation about the swimming axis turns a body-fixed asymmetry into a helix about a straight mean path, which is how many ciliates, flagellates and bacteria actually swim. They are not unable to steer: they bias the helix, reverse cilia or tumble to change direction.

Many molluscan and foraminiferal shells, and a good number of ruminant horns, are close to logarithmic spirals. Floret rows in a sunflower follow a generative Fermat spiral, not an equiangular one, so the claim that all of these permanent spirals are logarithmic is false.

A deflecting force of fixed direction, such as gravity or wind, bends a growing axis toward a limiting orientation and does not keep winding it into a spiral; the asymmetry has to turn with the growing tip. The snail's columellar muscle is not that force; coiling is produced by unequal growth around the mantle edge.

If a tube grows at a constant ratio of longitudinal to transverse extension and the two sides grow unequally, the generating curve is an equiangular spiral whose angle is fixed by that ratio. The circle and the straight line are the limiting cases, as stated.

Equal turning angles and a constant ratio of successive lengths make the shoots tangent to a logarithmic spiral, and a superimposed twist hides the same curve in a helicoid cyme. Real scorpioid cymes, such as those of the borage family, approximate those rules rather than meeting them exactly.

Self-similarity under enlargement is a defining property of the logarithmic spiral and, among ordinary plane curves, of no other. Many shells and horns nearly keep their shape while adding at the tip, but allometry is common both in the shell and in the animal, so constant shape is an idealisation.

On a true logarithmic spiral built by terminal addition, each new increment is a gnomon: the enlarged whole is similar to the previous whole. Horns, shells and chambered tests that actually grow that way satisfy the description; forms that are only roughly spiral do so only approximately.

A logarithmic spiral generated as a gnomonic accretion belongs to retained hard parts such as shell, horn, tusk and claw, which usually also show growth lines. Simultaneously formed outlines, such as a leaf margin or a fish profile, are not produced that way and are not generally equiangular spirals, though nothing forbids a soft contour from happening to fit one.

In a regularly coiled logarithmic shell, whorl breadths along a radius form a geometric progression, and in Nautilus each whorl is about three times the breadth of the previous one. Many ammonoids and gastropods are close to that rule, with clear exceptions where the expansion rate changes during growth.

A threefold increase in radius per whorl corresponds to an equiangular angle of about 80°, so the Nautilus figure is right. Ordinary ammonoids and many tightly coiled gastropods fall near 80–85°, but more rapidly expanding or irregularly coiled shells lie outside that band.

The coiled form of a univalve is fixed by the generating curve and by its rates of expansion, rotation and translation along the axis, together with its tilt. Differences among plain coiled shells are differences of degree in those factors, though sculpture, apertures and ontogenetic breaks are further differences of form.

The ratio of growth on the outer and inner sides of the tube is a principal control of whether successive whorls gape, touch or overlap, including the contrast between evolute and involute nautiloids. Umbilical width and the shape and position of the generating curve also affect overlap, so that ratio is not the only cause.

Spire height is largely the apical angle set by translation along the axis, while the equiangular spiral angle records radial versus tangential growth, and those are separable. High-spired Cerithium and flat Planorbis do not in fact share nearly the same spiral angle; the apical angle is not the only important difference among those shells.

Heteromorph ammonoids change coiling through life: some tighten the whorl expansion, and Scaphites, Ancyloceras and Lituites open the late shell toward a hook or a straight shaft. Describing that opening as a progressive fall of the spiral angle toward the straight-line limit is geometrically appropriate.

A larger or smaller spiral angle does not say which shell is ancestral, and an intermediate angle is not evidence of an intermediate stage of descent. Similar coiled and uncoiled cephalopod shells have arisen more than once, so series built only from those grades are not supported.

Some fossil lineages show sustained, directional change in growth ratios, and a low-dimensional description of form can make such a trend visible. The same description shows that nearly identical shapes can be reached independently, so a strong resemblance need not be a single inherited series.

Bivalve and brachiopod growth lines spread from the umbo rather than sitting as concentric circles about an interior point, and they record a growth rate that varies with direction. Circular arcs through the umbo fit simple shells such as Anomia only approximately; more elongated shells need a richer directional rule than a single coaxial family.

Clam shrimps retain successive carapaces instead of shedding them completely, so the old margins remain as growth lines on a bivalved shell that resembles a small mollusc. The outline is an accretionary spiral of low expansion; calling it a logarithmic spiral of small angle is a fair description of that valve.

Laterally directed spiralia are typical of transverse spiriferids, and more rounded atrypid shells carry differently oriented cones, so a coarse association with shell shape exists. The brachidium is a secreted skeletal support with its own developmental pattern, not a coil whose direction is fixed by passive pressure in the mantle cavity.

Aptychi are ammonoid jaws, sometimes also covering the aperture, and are not the dorsal half of a shell split from the coiled whorl. The external shell of Nautilus and the internal shells of Sepia and Spirula are homologous dorsal shells, not the two leftover pieces of that split cone.

A simple nautiloid septum is close to a spherical cap, as expected for a membrane under fairly uniform pressure with a plain attachment, and sinuous attachment produces saddle-shaped regions. Ammonitic septa are not soap films of least area; a pressurised membrane has constant mean curvature, and fluted septa are further organised by the mantle.

Finely branched ammonitic sutures end in rounded lobules and look something like dendritic wetting patterns. That resemblance does not show that the frilling is the same surface-tension instability as milk on a greasy plate; septal folding is a morphogenetic process in the mantle–shell system.

Closely similar logarithmic shells recur in gastropods, cephalopods, foraminifera and tube worms, and across many geological periods. Form is not almost unrelated to the animal or to habitat: the groups remain distinguishable, and environment biases which coil shapes are common.

Once the growth ratios are fixed, the logarithmic varieties follow from geometry without a further selective sculpting of each whorl. Which ratios persist in populations is partly a consequence of selection and of functional performance, so selection is not dispensable in accounting for the forms that actually occur.

A free fluid drop is spherical, and some single-chambered foraminifera, such as Orbulina, are spheres whose outline is consistent with surface tension. Many unilocular tests are flask-shaped, tubular or ornamented, which are not equilibrium drop shapes frozen at secretion.

Adding permanent chambers on the outside, with the aperture advancing around the test, does produce spiral foraminifera, and that mode of growth is common. The same external accretion also yields straight uniserial, biserial and irregular tests, so permanent increments favour spirals only when the growth direction itself rotates.

Regularly coiled foraminifera are approximately logarithmic spirals: the many-chambered test is nearly the same shape as the young test. Chamber shape and the expansion rate often change through ontogeny, so continued similarity is typical rather than exact.

A whorl-to-whorl breadth ratio of 1.5 corresponds to an equiangular angle of about 86°, so that part of the statement is exact and matches the slow expansion of ammonoid-like spirals. A single ratio near 1.5 is plausible for some fusulinid species but is not a constant for the genus.

Chamber volumes often increase in a roughly constant ratio, which is what exponential growth proportional to existing mass would produce in a uniform test. Many foraminifera depart from a constant ratio, and chamber size is regulated at each addition rather than entailed by bulk homogeneity alone.

Foraminiferal chamber faces are generally convex in the direction of growth, whereas nautiloid septa are concave toward the living chamber, matching membranes loaded from opposite sides. Both are only approximately least-area or constant-mean-curvature surfaces once the attachment line is complicated.

Similar successive chambers whose sizes stay in a constant ratio do form a logarithmic spiral, and a single fixed contact angle is too narrow to explain the variety of coils. Minimum potential energy does not by itself place each new chamber or make it similar to the last; chamber position is developmentally specified.
